1.text:
Why Is Earth Still Active While Its Neighbors Went Quiet?

In Deck 4 you learned why the inner planets are small and rocky: they formed inside the frost line. Now you get to meet them one at a time. There are five rocky worlds in the inner solar system: Mercury, Venus, Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Here's the puzzle. All five were built from the same disk at about the same time. So why did they turn out so different? Earth still has volcanoes, moving plates, oceans, and weather. Its neighbors mostly went quiet a long time ago. As you'll see, three big things made the difference: a world's size, its distance from the Sun, and its atmosphere.

Before you turn the page, take one minute and make a prediction. Earth, Venus, and Mars formed at the same time. Write down one way each is different today, and why you think so.

Did you know? The five dots on this page are the five worlds in order, drawn to the right sizes (but not the right distances). Can you guess which is which?

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's the plan for this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements so you can check yourself at the end.

I can describe the size, interior, surface, and air of each rocky world. I can explain why a small world cools fast and goes quiet. I can name the 4 shapers: impacts, volcanism, tectonics, and erosion. I can explain the Moon's maria and how the Moon formed. I can explain Venus's runaway greenhouse. I can use evidence for water on Mars, past and present. I can model Earth's layers and explain why Earth is still active. And I can use Earth as the "control planet" for comparisons in Q2.

That's eight goals, each tagged with an Indiana standard or marked as enrichment. Rate yourself 1 to 3 on each now, and again at the end.

3.text:
Meet the Terrestrial Worlds

A terrestrial world is a rocky world with three layers: an iron core, a rocky mantle, and a thin crust. Those layers sorted themselves out early on, when the young worlds were hot enough to melt. Heavy metal sank and lighter rock floated up.

Here they are, drawn to scale. Mercury is 4,879 km across. Venus is 12,104 km. Earth is 12,756 km. The Moon is 3,475 km. And Mars is 6,792 km. So Venus is almost exactly Earth's size, Mars is about half, Mercury is a bit more than a third, and the Moon is only about a quarter.

Picture Earth as a basketball. Then Venus is a slightly smaller ball, Mars is a softball, Mercury is about baseball-sized, and the Moon is a tennis ball.

Did you know? Earth is the densest planet in the solar system, partly because its large mass squeezes its insides together.

4.text:
Small Worlds Cool Fast

Volcanoes and moving crust need energy from inside a planet. That internal heat comes from two places. Some is heat left over from when the world formed. The rest comes from radioactive decay, which is still heating planets today. Internal heat is what powers geology.

But heat slowly leaks out through the surface, and that's where size matters. A small world has a lot of surface compared to its insides, so it cools fast. Think of a pea and a baked potato fresh out of the oven. The pea is cool in a minute, while the potato stays hot for a long time.

Look at the slide. A large world stays hot inside, with radioactive decay heating its core. A small world has already cooled, and its heat escaped to space. The Moon and Mercury cooled long ago. Mars stayed active longer but is mostly quiet now. Earth and Venus are still hot inside.

Did you know? Sunlight only warms a planet's surface and air. It never heats the core.

5.text:
What Shapes a Surface

Only 4 processes shape the surface of every rocky world. Learn these four and you can "read" any planet's face.

Impact cratering: asteroids and comets blast out bowl-shaped craters. More craters means an older surface. Volcanism: melted rock rises up from inside and erupts as lava, building volcanoes and burying old craters. Tectonics: forces from inside stretch, squeeze, or crack the crust, making cliffs, valleys, and mountains. Erosion: wind, water, ice, and gravity wear rock down and carry it away.

Notice what each one depends on. Volcanism and tectonics need internal heat, so they depend on a world's size. Erosion needs an atmosphere. Impacts happen everywhere, but they only stick around where the other three haven't erased them.

Did you know? Erosion isn't just water. Wind, ice, gravity, and even tiny space dust can wear rock away.

6.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Let's see if Part 1 clicked. Which world stays geologically active the longest?

Is it A) the largest one, because it keeps its internal heat, B) the closest to the Sun, because sunlight heats its core, C) the one with the most craters, or D) the smallest one, because it cools evenly?

Think back to the pea and the potato on Slide 4. Pick your answer and be ready to explain why the others don't work.

7.text:
Mercury: An Iron World

Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest one to the Sun. It's only a little bigger than our Moon. Inside, though, they're nothing alike. Mercury's density is 5,429 kg/m³, almost as high as Earth's. The Moon's is only 3,340 kg/m³.

Since Mercury is small, its insides aren't squeezed much. So that high density means it must be made mostly of iron. The NASA MESSENGER mission found that Mercury's iron core takes up about 85% of its radius, and part of it is still molten. The rocky shell on top is only about 400 km thick.

That partly melted core gives Mercury something Venus and Mars don't have: a weak magnetic field, about 1% as strong as Earth's.

Did you know? Mercury spins 3 times for every 2 trips around the Sun. One full day, from sunrise to sunrise, lasts about 176 Earth days.

8.text:
Why So Much Iron? 3 Ideas

Here's a real mystery scientists are still working on. Mercury's core takes up about 85% of its radius. That's one big core. How did it get that way?

There are three ideas. Idea 1: a giant impact blasted away Mercury's outer layers. Idea 2: Mercury got baked by the Sun, which boiled off its outer rock. Idea 3: Mercury was built from metal to begin with, because so close to the Sun, mostly metal could turn solid.

Which idea do you think explains it? Vote, and write down one reason before you turn the page.

9.text:
Why So Much Iron? The Clue

Here's a clue from the MESSENGER spacecraft. Mercury's crust still holds easy-to-boil elements, like potassium and sulfur.

Think about what that means. If the Sun had baked off Mercury's outer rock, those easy-to-boil elements would be long gone. So Idea 2, baked by the Sun, is less likely.

What about the other two? Ideas 1 and 3, the giant impact and the metal building blocks, are still being tested. Did the clue change your vote? That's normal in science: an idea gains or loses support as new evidence comes in.

10.text:
Mercury's Shrinking Crust

From far away, Mercury looks a lot like the Moon, with craters everywhere. But look closer and you'll find something odd: long, curving cliffs, some up to about 3 km (almost 2 miles) high. These are called lobate scarps.

Here's how they formed. As Mercury's huge iron core cooled, it shrank, and the whole planet got smaller. The stiff crust didn't have room, so it cracked. One block of crust got shoved up over another along a crack called a thrust fault. Follow the before-and-after on the slide. It's like the wrinkles that form on an apple as it dries out.

This is tectonics without moving plates. Mercury's crust is all one piece. Its volcanoes shut down early because the small planet cooled fast, and with no air, there's no erosion.

Did you know? These cliffs cut right across older craters, so scientists know the cliffs formed later.

11.text:
Ice on the Planet Nearest the Sun?

Here's a question that sounds like a trick. Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. Its daytime temperatures can reach 430 °C, hot enough to melt lead.

So could the planet closest to the Sun have ice? Yes or no?

Make your prediction, and write down one reason for it before you turn the page.

12.text:
Ice on the Planet Nearest the Sun? The Answer

Yes! Mercury has ice. It's hidden in craters near its poles, where the crater floors sit in forever-shadow. Sunlight never reaches them, so they stay frozen.

Radar spotted it. The ice shows up bright in radar images. It was first seen by radar in 1991 and later confirmed by the MESSENGER spacecraft.

If you said no because Mercury is "too hot," that's a sensible reason. It just turns out that being close to the Sun doesn't heat places the sunlight never touches.

Did you know? The best time to spot Mercury in our sky is just before sunrise or just after sunset.

13.text:
The Moon's Face

Look at a full Moon and you'll see bright areas and dark patches. The bright parts are the highlands: the Moon's oldest crust, covered with craters. The dark patches are called maria, which is Latin for "seas." Early astronomers thought they were oceans!

They're not water, though. Maria are dark lava plains that flooded giant impact basins. Follow the steps on the slide. First, a huge impact dug out a basin hundreds of kilometers wide. Later, melted rock rose up through the cracked floor and filled it with dark lava. That happened between about 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago.

The maria have far fewer craters than the highlands, so they're younger. Then the small Moon cooled, its volcanoes stopped, and with no air or water, nothing wears its surface down. The Moon is basically a museum of the early solar system, with nobody around to dust it.

Did you know? The "man in the Moon" or "rabbit in the Moon" that people see is made of the maria.

14.text:
How the Moon Formed

You met this story in Deck 4. Now let's add what Moon rocks tell us. Step 1: about 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body called Theia hit the young Earth. Step 2: the debris formed a ring, and the Moon gathered from it.

Step 3: all that energy melted the Moon's outer layers into a magma ocean, a global sea of molten rock hundreds of kilometers deep. Step 4: as the magma ocean cooled, heavy minerals sank and light rock floated up to the top. That light rock became the bright highland crust.

The evidence fits. Apollo astronauts brought back 382 kg of samples, and the highland rocks are exactly the light, floating kind this story predicts.

Did you know? You can model step 4 by shaking oil and colored water in a bottle and letting it settle. The lighter liquid floats to the top.

15.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Here's a puzzle. The Moon is covered in craters, but Earth has very few. Why does the Moon have far more craters than Earth?

Is it A) Earth erased its craters with erosion, lava, and plates, B) the Moon is a bigger target than Earth, C) Earth's air stops every incoming rock, or D) impacts began only after Earth had formed?

Look back at the four shapers on Slide 5 before you choose. Be ready to use the words "older" and "craters" in your answer.

16.text:
Venus: Earth's Hot Twin

Venus is almost Earth's twin. It's nearly the same size and has nearly the same gravity, and it formed in the same part of the disk. But don't plan a vacation there.

The air pressure on Venus's surface is 92 bars, 92 times Earth's. That's like being about 930 m under the sea. The surface temperature is 464 °C, hot enough to melt lead. The air is thick carbon dioxide (CO₂), and the clouds are made of sulfuric acid.

Those bright clouds reflect most of the sunlight that hits them, which is why Venus shines so brightly in our sky. So how did Earth's twin turn out so different? The answer is on the next page.

Did you know? Soviet Venera landers that reached Venus's surface lasted from minutes to about two hours before the heat and pressure destroyed them.

17.text:
The Runaway Greenhouse

Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor let sunlight in but trap heat. A little greenhouse effect is a good thing. Without it, Earth's average temperature would be below freezing.

On young Venus, the effect ran away. Follow the loop on the slide. Sunlight warms the surface. Oceans evaporate. Water vapor traps more heat. It gets hotter, so even more water evaporates. Round and round it goes, and every lap makes the next one worse. Venus gets about 1.9 times as much sunlight as Earth, which gave the loop an extra push.

High in the air, sunlight broke apart the water molecules, and the light hydrogen escaped to space. The water was lost for good, but the CO₂ stayed. On Earth, liquid water helps lock CO₂ away in rocks like limestone. With no oceans, Venus couldn't do that, so its air filled up with CO₂.

Did you know? Scientists think the Sun is slowly brightening, and it could push Earth into a runaway greenhouse in roughly 1 billion years.

18.text:
Venus: New Skin, No Plates

Venus's thick clouds hide its surface, but radar can see right through them. In the early 1990s, NASA's Magellan spacecraft mapped about 98% of Venus with radar. It found volcanoes everywhere, plus strange flat-topped "pancake domes" made of thick, sticky lava.

Surprisingly, Venus has fairly few impact craters. That means its surface is young. Huge lava floods covered the planet and buried the old craters, a process called resurfacing.

But Venus has no moving plates. Its crust acts as one piece. A leading idea is that without water, Venus's rock is too stiff to break into plates. Scientists are still testing that, and new missions in the 2030s aim to find out more.

Did you know? Venus is still hot inside, and NASA says it may still have active volcanoes.

19.text:
Venus's Friendly Sky

You know the surface of Venus is a furnace: 92 bars and 464 °C. But things change as you go up.

About 50 to 55 km above the surface, inside the clouds, the air pressure is about 1 bar, close to Earth's at sea level. The temperature there is about 30 to 75 °C. That's a hot summer day up to the temperature of very hot tap water.

It still wouldn't be a nice place to breathe, though. There's no oxygen (O₂), and the clouds are made of sulfuric acid.

20.text:
Mars: Volcanoes and Canyons

Mars is in the middle: about half of Earth's size. Being mid-sized, it stayed hot inside longer than the Moon and Mercury. That was long enough to build the biggest volcanoes in the solar system, though it has since cooled down.

The champion is Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the solar system. It dwarfs Mount Everest (and the drawing isn't to scale). It sits near the Tharsis volcanoes, a line of giant volcanoes. Mars volcanoes grew so huge because Mars has no moving plates. The same hot spot kept erupting in the same place for a very long time.

Then there's Valles Marineris, a canyon system on Mars about 4,000 km long and up to about 7 km deep. That's long enough to stretch from California to New York, and about 9 times longer than the Grand Canyon. It's mostly a giant crack in the crust that opened as the Tharsis region bulged upward.

Did you know? Mars is red because its dust is full of iron oxide, which is rust. It's actually very cold, about minus 65 °C on average.

21.text:
Water on Mars: Then and Now

Mars today is a cold desert, and its air is too thin for lakes. Liquid water quickly freezes or evaporates. Billions of years ago, though, it looked very different.

Look at the left side of the slide. Scientists have found ancient river valleys, lakebeds, and deltas. A delta is a fan of sediment dropped where a river flows into a lake. The best example is in Jezero crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover has been exploring since landing in 2021. A river once flowed into a lake there.

So where's the water now? Look at the right side. Some is frozen in the polar ice caps, and some is ice hiding just under the soil. In 2008, the Phoenix lander scraped up real water ice in the Martian arctic.

Did you know? Perseverance is collecting rock samples from Jezero that might one day be brought back to Earth.

22.text:
Where Did Mars's Air Go?

If early Mars had thick air, where did it go? NASA's MAVEN spacecraft found a big part of the answer. The solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, strips away about 100 g of Mars's air every second. That's about a quarter pound.

That doesn't sound like much, but it adds up over billions of years. Compare the numbers on the slide: Earth's surface air pressure is 1,014 mb (millibars), while Mars's is only 6 mb.

Why Mars and not Earth? Mars has no global magnetic field to shield it from the solar wind. It had one about 4 billion years ago, but it shut off as the small planet's core cooled. Here's the chain: small planet, core cools, magnetic field dies, solar wind strips the air, planet gets colder and drier.

Did you know? Mars still has a thin atmosphere, with clouds, wind, and huge dust storms.

23.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Venus and Earth are almost the same size. So why is Venus 464 °C?

Is it because A) its thick CO₂ air traps heat in a runaway greenhouse, B) it's closer to the Sun than Mercury is, C) its core is much hotter than Earth's core, or D) its volcanoes are erupting everywhere today?

Take a minute to think quietly, then vote. Be ready to explain your choice using the loop from Slide 17.

24.text:
Inside Earth

Earth has four main layers. On top is the crust, a thin outer skin of rock. Below it is the mantle, about 2,900 km of hot rock. The mantle is solid, but over millions of years it flows slowly, like very stiff putty.

Deeper down is the outer core: Earth's liquid iron layer. As Earth spins, that liquid metal churns, and its flow makes Earth's magnetic field. At the very center is the inner core, a solid ball of iron and nickel. It's extremely hot, but the pressure is so high that it stays solid.

That magnetic field shields us from the solar wind. Remember Mars, which lost its field and much of its air? Also, the whole Earth has a density of 5,514 kg/m³, much higher than surface rock. That proves heavy metal is packed deep inside.

Did you know? A hard-boiled egg cut in half makes a decent model: the shell is the crust, the white is the mantle, and the yolk is the core. Real crust is even thinner than an eggshell, though!

25.text:
Why Earth Is Still Active

Plate tectonics means Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into plates that slowly move. Earth is the only one of the five worlds still reshaping itself this way. Part of the reason is size: Earth is the largest rocky world, so it kept the most internal heat.

That heat keeps the mantle slowly churning, a motion called mantle convection. Follow the slide. At a ridge, plates pull apart and new seafloor forms. At a subduction zone, one plate sinks back down into the mantle. These plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow, just a few centimeters a year.

Water helps too. Scientists think liquid water weakens rock enough to let it break into plates, which may be why Earth has plates and dry Venus doesn't. All of this keeps Earth's surface young. The oldest seafloor is less than about 200 million years old.

Did you know? Almost all of Earth's craters have been erased, even though Earth is 4.54 billion years old.

26.text:
Q2 Preview: Earth Is the Control

In an experiment, the control is the normal case you compare everything to. In planetary science, Earth is the control planet, the yardstick for every other world. We understand Earth best, so we learn about other worlds by asking how they're different.

Compare the three columns. Venus is too hot at 464 °C, with no plates and no oceans. Earth is 15 °C, with liquid oceans and moving plates. Mars is too cold at minus 65 °C, with thin air and ice.

Every Q2 deck will end with a Venus vs Earth vs Mars comparison. Start a three-column page in your notebook now and fill in these rows. You'll keep adding to it all quarter.

Did you know? Distance from the Sun isn't the whole story. Atmosphere and size matter just as much, as you saw with Venus and Mars.

Time to build a model. Draw Earth's 4 layers to scale. Then add the Moon and Mars at the same scale.

For each of Earth's layers, write down its physical and chemical properties. Is it solid or liquid? What is it made of?

28.text:
Exit Ticket

You just toured five whole worlds. Show what you've got with three quick questions.

First, why did the Moon go quiet while Earth is still active? Second, name one piece of evidence that Mars once had liquid water. Third, what is a runaway greenhouse? Use Venus as your example.

When you're done, look back at the prediction you wrote on Slide 1. How did your thinking change? Then rate yourself 1 to 3 on each "I can" statement from Slide 2.

29.text:
One More Question

Here's a bonus question to stretch your thinking. Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. How can it still hold ice?

Explain it, and name the evidence that shows the ice is really there.

30.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.2.2: describe the different kinds of objects in the solar system, including planets, moons, comets, asteroids, and protoplanets. Know that planets have been found orbiting other stars, and even drifting with no star at all. And describe how our solar system is organized, from the rocky and giant planets to the asteroid belt and the Oort Cloud.

ES.6.1: build a diagram or model of Earth's crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core, and describe what each is like and what it's made of. This deck gives you a first look, and Deck 9 goes all the way.
